clue.text: Wear diamonds, entering a bank in Glasgow

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the item that enters something ends up sitting inside it

parts.note: brae is the Scots word for a hillside or bank
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: Someone in Glasgow sports diamond jewellery on a visit to the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: D goes inside A BRAE to make ABRADE; brae is a Scottish word for a slope, hence 'in Glasgow'.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear something down is to abrade it, rubbing away its surface by friction.

clue.text: Noble god, over time, displaying eternal youth

indicators.note: in a down clue one word sits over another by straddling it, so it wraps around the next item

parts.note: a peer is a member of the nobility
T is the standard abbreviation for time
Pan is the Greek god of the wild

explanation.surface: A lordly deity, despite the passing years, still looks forever young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noble god' reads as one divine aristocrat, but it is two separate pieces with time slipped into the first.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's character is the boy who never grows up, the archetype of perpetual boyhood.

clue.text: People like Thomas Cook used to blather vacuously

indicators.note: to cook figures is to fiddle them, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, the word keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of blather

explanation.surface: The travel agent Thomas Cook once had a habit of talking empty nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thomas Cook' reads as the travel firm's founder, but Thomas ends the definition and Cook starts the wordplay. Doubting Thomas is the apostle who would not believe in the resurrection without proof.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle Thomas famously refused to believe without seeing, so people of his sceptical kind are doubters.

clue.text: One tends to fire small person smoking marijuana, say

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a toker takes a toke, a puff on a joint; marijuana is just one example of what is smoked

explanation.surface: A little guy who smokes pot is prone to getting the sack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tends to fire' looks like 'is inclined to dismiss', but tends means looks after: the definition is someone who feeds a furnace.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoker's job is feeding and tending the furnace of a steam engine or boiler.

clue.text: Area by border invaded by servicemen in WWII battle

indicators.note: a place that is invaded has an occupying force inside it

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area
the Royal Navy, the UK's naval service
a hem is the edge of a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: A frontier region overrun by troops in a famous Second World War fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The military surface fits the answer exactly, so the wordplay hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1944 Battle of Arnhem in the Netherlands was the Allied airborne assault of Operation Market Garden.

clue.text: Zero added to fifty plus one for English mathematician

parts.note: love means zero in tennis scoring
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
an ace is the one in a deck of cards

explanation.surface: Simple sums in a clue for a famous numerical thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Ada Lovelace wrote what is often called the first computer program, for Babbage's Analytical Engine.

clue.text: Give me strength and energy to shelter in oases in desert

indicators.note: something that shelters in a place is enclosed by it
the second 'in' places the combined result inside the following word

parts.note: to desert someone is to forsake them
an oasis is a refuge, a haven
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A weary traveller in the desert pleads for the strength to reach shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like sand dunes beside the oases, but it is the verb meaning abandon, and it wraps the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exasperated exclamations, said when someone's patience is being sorely tried.

clue.text: Youngster wanting good story book tucked into treat and drink

indicators.note: something tucked into another thing is placed inside it

parts.note: to treat an illness is to cure it
B is the abbreviation for book
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A child keen on a good tale settles down with a book, a snack and a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Youngster wanting good story' reads like a child at bedtime, but the story is a news scoop.
explanation.definitionFit: A cub reporter is a novice journalist, always hungry for a scoop to make their name.

clue.text: Without rumpy-pumpy, romancing is possibly a brief activity?

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so these letters go round the other item
possibly suggests one of several possible arrangements of the letters

parts.note: taken as written
rumpy-pumpy is jokey British slang for sex

explanation.surface: Courtship without the bedroom part, it is suggested, might be a fleeting fling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside: the rearranged letters wrap round SEX. A brief is a barrister, and questioning witnesses is what one does in court.
explanation.definitionFit: In legal slang a brief is a barrister, and questioning the opposing side's witness is a barrister's courtroom work.

clue.text: Triumphant exclamation upright character ignored in US state

indicators.note: a letter that is ignored is left out of the word

parts.note: the Midwestern state
the letter I is a single vertical stroke

explanation.surface: A victorious cry from an honest person goes unheard in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from OHIO. 'Upright character' looks like an honest person, but it is the letter shaped like a single stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: Oho is an interjection of gleeful surprise or triumph, as when catching someone out.

clue.text: Nabokov — a tease, somewhat elliptical

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the following words is used

parts.note: the run of letters spans the end of the novelist's name and the next two words

explanation.surface: A critic finds the author Nabokov a bit of a teasing, evasive writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovate means egg-shaped, an oval form that is roughly elliptical.

clue.text: That lady cooks cakes, given hot tip

parts.note: what you do to cakes when cooking them
the pronoun for a woman
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A woman bakes, and someone hands her a useful kitchen hint.
explanation.walkthrough: Tip here means a gratuity, not a piece of kitchen advice.
explanation.definitionFit: Baksheesh is a small sum given as a gratuity or bribe in parts of the Middle East and South Asia.

clue.text: Gently drilling metal base for tall structure

indicators.note: a drill bores into material, so this goes inside the next item

parts.note: steel is an alloy of iron
p for piano, the musical direction to play softly
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: Carefully boring into a metal base to erect a tall building.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes inside STEEL, then E follows. e is the mathematical constant used as the base of natural logs.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tall pointed tower of a church.

clue.text: Sweet Polish-American bagging business qualification

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it inside a bag, enclosing it

parts.note: to polish a surface is to rub it
A is the abbreviation for American
Master of Business Administration

explanation.surface: A sweet-natured Polish-American gains a management degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' with its capital looks like a nationality, but it is the verb meaning to buff a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A rum baba is a small yeast cake soaked in rum syrup, served as a dessert.

clue.text: Times setter's seen cryptic crossword setter

parts.note: x is the multiplication sign, read as times

indicators.note: cryptic means obscured or puzzling, so the word is scrambled

parts.note: the setter is 'I', so setter's is I'M
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Times compiler has spotted a famous puzzle-maker's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times setter' looks like a compiler for The Times newspaper, but Times is the multiplication sign. Ximenes set the Observer's cryptic puzzle and wrote the rules many setters follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Ximenes was the pseudonym of D. S. Macnutt, the Observer compiler whose principles shaped fair cryptic cluing.

clue.text: Above isle, spots shooting star?

parts.note: spots and marks are both blemishes
the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: Looking down on an island, someone watches a meteor streak by.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'Above' sets the order. 'Shooting star' sounds like a meteor, but it means someone who stars at shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: A marksman is an expert shot, the star performer at shooting a gun.

clue.text: My acceleration due to gravity checked by device used when driving train

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: something checked is held in, so it is enclosed by what follows

parts.note: golfers drive the ball off a tee
g is the physics symbol for this

explanation.surface: A worried note about gravity being tested on a train's driving equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving' suggests a train driver, but it is golf, where the ball is driven from a peg.
explanation.definitionFit: A cortege is a solemn procession, especially at a funeral; train in its sense of a following line of people.

clue.text: E.g. Mary Beard gives away one First from Cambridge for discriminating type

indicators.note: what is given away is lost from the word

parts.note: Mary Beard is a well-known Cambridge scholar of ancient Rome
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the first letter of the next word is the one taken

parts.note: the opening letter of Cambridge

explanation.surface: A Cambridge don renounces a top degree and is called a snob.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the run IC from CLASSICIST. 'First from Cambridge' looks like a top-class degree, but it just means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A classist is someone who discriminates against people on grounds of social class.

clue.text: Brilliant quality of artist, one inspired by art

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician

indicators.note: something inspired is breathed in, so it goes inside the next item

parts.note: dance is one of the performing arts
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An artist's brilliance, fired by art itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Radiance is brightness or glowing brilliance, whether of light or of a person's happiness.

clue.text: Bit of a joint model rolled inhaled by utopian writer

indicators.note: something inhaled is drawn inside the one breathing

parts.note: Sir Thomas More wrote Utopia

indicators.note: a thing rolled over is turned the other way round

parts.note: to sit for an artist is to model

explanation.surface: A smoker rolls a joint and an idealist takes a drag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint', 'rolled' and 'inhaled' paint a cannabis scene, but the joint is in carpentry.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortise is the recess cut into timber to receive a tenon in a mortise-and-tenon woodworking joint.

clue.text: Encourage coitus, wearing nice pants

indicators.note: what is wearing something is covered by it, so goes inside
pants is British slang for rubbish, so the word is mangled

parts.note: taken as written
'it' is a coy euphemism for sex

explanation.surface: Urging a partner into bed while wearing attractive underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like underwear; here it is the British slang for poor or rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: To incite is to urge or stir someone up to act.

clue.text: Product that's often shipped from Ostia Antica or Canopus, say?

parts.note: ex means from, as in ex works
both were harbours of the ancient world, at Rome and in Egypt

explanation.surface: Goods dispatched from ancient Mediterranean harbours.
explanation.walkthrough: Ostia was the port of ancient Rome; Canopus was an Egyptian harbour city near Alexandria.
explanation.definitionFit: An export is a commodity sent abroad for sale, typically by ship.

clue.text: Old magistrates awfully idle, in the main, after retiring

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the word reads from right to left
the jumbled letters are placed inside the following word

parts.note: the main is a poetic term for the open sea

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Former officials who were mostly lazy once they had retired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' reads as 'mostly', but main is the sea. Aediles were Roman officials in charge of public buildings and games.
explanation.definitionFit: Aediles were magistrates of ancient Rome responsible for public works, markets and games.

clue.text: This person wears coat of Leatherette, sound like a cow hide

indicators.note: the wearer is inside the clothing, so it goes within
a coat is the outside layer, so only the outer letters are used

parts.note: the first and last letters of Leatherette
the setter refers to themself
to low is to moo

explanation.surface: Someone dressed in fake leather tries to make a mooing noise, like a cowhide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' seems to finish the cowhide picture, but it is a verb: to stay out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie low is to keep out of sight and avoid attention, which is to hide.

clue.text: Supplier of eggs and mushrooms receiving a confirmation request from abroad

parts.note: eggs are laid and found in a nest

indicators.note: whatever receives something takes it in, so it holds it inside

parts.note: ceps are porcini mushrooms
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shop selling eggs and mushrooms takes a phone call asking to check an order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplier of eggs' suggests a farm or a hen, but it is where eggs sit.
explanation.definitionFit: N'est-ce pas is French for 'isn't it?', a tag question seeking agreement.

clue.text: Leader of pack seen in two lakes side by side

indicators.note: only what is seen inside the pair is kept, so the outer letters are dropped

parts.note: the word lake written twice running

explanation.surface: A wolf-pack leader is spotted between two adjoining lakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are not printed in a row in the clue: write out the word twice and read across the join, losing the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Akela is the adult leader of a Cub Scout pack, named after the wolf in Kipling's Jungle Book.

clue.text: Prohibit cycling league in America

indicators.note: the letters go round in rotation, the last moving to the front

parts.note: to prohibit is to ban

explanation.surface: A ban on a bike-racing league in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the final letter of BAN to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The NBA is the National Basketball Association, the professional basketball league of the USA.

clue.text: Perhaps the creative force behind Tango and Sprite changed job

definitions.text: Perhaps the creative force behind Tango

indicators.note: a changed word has its letters put into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
a chore is a routine task

explanation.surface: An ad agency creative behind two fizzy-drink brands, Tango and Sprite, switches jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Tango and Sprite look like a pair of soft drinks, but the definition ends at Tango, the dance; Tango is a British orange soda.
explanation.definitionFit: Terpsichore is the Greek Muse of dance, so she might be said to inspire the tango.
